# 18.1.2  Model fitting

To fit the model, we need to minimize the following loss:

$$\mathcal{L}(\theta)=\sum_{j=1}^{J}\sum_{x_i\in R_j}\ell(y_i,w_j)$$  
(18.2)

Unfortunately, this is not differentiable, because of the need to learn the discrete tree structure. Indeed, finding the optimal partitioning of the data is NP-complete [HR76]. The standard practice is to use a greedy procedure, in which we iteratively grow the tree one node at a time. This approach is used by CART [BF084], C4.5 [Qui93], and ID3 [Qui86], which are three popular implementations of the method.

The idea is as follows. Suppose we are at node $i$, and let $D_i=\{(x_n,y_n)\in N_i\}$ be the set of examples that reach this node. Let $D_i^L(j,t)=\{(x_n,y_n)\in N_i:y_{n,j}\le t\}$ and $D_i^R(j,t)=\{(x_n,y_n)\in N_i:y_{n,j}>t\}$ be a partition of these examples into left and right subtrees. (For categorical features, we use $D_i^L(j,t)=\{(x_n,y_n)\in N_i:y_{n,j}=t\}$ and $D_i^R(j,t)=\{(x_n,y_n)\in N_i:y_{n,j}\ne t\}$.) We choose the best feature $j_i$ to split on, and the best value for that feature, $t_i$, as follows:

$$(j_i,t_i)=\arg\min_{j\in\{1,\ldots,D\}}\min_{t\in\mathcal{T}_j}\frac{|D_i^L(j,t)|}{|D|}c(D_i^L(j,t))+\frac{|D_i^R(j,t)|}{|D|}c(D_i^R(j,t))$$  
(18.3)

where the cost function $c()$ is defined below.

The set of possible thresholds $\mathcal{T}_j$ for feature $j$ can be obtained by sorting the unique values of $\{x_{nj}\}$. For example, if feature 1 has the values $\{4.5,-12,72,-12\}$, then we set $\mathcal{T}_1=\{-12,4.5,72\}$. In the case of categorical inputs, we consider each unique value of $\{x_{nj}\}$. (Although we could allow for multi-way splits, resulting in non-binary trees, this may cause **data fragmentation**, in which too little data might “fall” into each subtree, resulting in overfitting.)

We now discuss the cost function $c(D_i)$ which is used to evaluate the cost of node $i$. For regression, we can use the mean squared error

$$\operatorname{cost}(D_i)=\frac{1}{|D_i|}\sum_{n\in D_i}(y_n-\bar{y})^2$$  
(18.4)
